info.name: OAS Auth Service
info.description:
The auth-service on :8080 and Keycloak on :8180.

Keycloak stores no passwords. It holds an identity shell per user — the userId plus org_id, entity_type and registries — and issues tokens for it. This service owns those tokens and their revocation.

Run the requests top to bottom. Bodies carry literal placeholders such as PASTE_USER_ID_HERE; replace them with values copied from the previous response. Every request description says what to copy and what to expect.

The core of it is Create Token, Validate Token and Invalidate Token. The rest exist to make those demonstrable and to cover the user lifecycle the catalogue drives.

CREDENTIAL VERIFICATION is flag-gated and OFF by default. With catalogue.validate-enabled=false, Create Token takes {userId} and trusts its caller — which is what this collection assumes. Set it to true, with catalogue.base-url pointing at the user-catalogue, and Create Token instead takes {username, password}, verifies them against the catalogue's /user/v1/verify, and issues nothing unless it answers valid:true. The last request here shows that body.

Because the default trusts its caller, none of these endpoints may be routed through Kong or any ingress.

Select the 'OAS Auth Service - Local' environment first.

request.description:
Confirms the service is up. Expect 200 with status UP.

Owns no database, so this depends only on the app itself — it stays UP even if Keycloak or Redis are down. Those failures surface on the endpoints below instead.

Provisions the user in Keycloak so tokens can be issued for them. The user-catalogue calls this when a record becomes ACTIVE.

Pick any userId you like and reuse it in every request below. Change it to run through again with a fresh user.

Expect 200 with created:true. Send it a second time and you get created:false — it is an upsert, because the catalogue retries a publish whose response it never saw.

`orgId` and `entityType` are required. `firstName`, `lastName`, `email` and `registries` are optional.

`registries` is the list of catalogues this user may use, and it reaches the token as a JSON ARRAY. It is three-state:
  omitted  -> whatever is already stored is kept
  []       -> cleared, and the claim disappears from the token entirely
  ["a","b"] -> replaced
Blanks and duplicates are dropped. The values come from whoever owns the permission matrix; this service only carries what it is given.

`email` is left out on purpose — Keycloak enforces unique addresses, so reusing one another userId already holds returns 409 AUTH_USER_CONFLICT, the one error retrying will never fix.

No password is sent. Keycloak stores no credential for these users at all.

Issues tokens for the user. Expect 200.

COPY result.access_token and result.refresh_token for the next requests.

Paste the access token into jwt.io. Alongside user_id, org_id and entity_type you should see registries as an array, plus given_name, family_name, name and email — those four come from Keycloak's built-in scopes, so they appear as soon as Create User supplies the fields.

This body is the default, TRUSTED mode: no password, and a token is minted for whatever userId is given. With catalogue.validate-enabled=true the body becomes {username, password} instead — see the last request — and a userId in the body is then IGNORED, so one valid password cannot mint a token for another account.

Run it before Create User and you get 404 AUTH_USER_NOT_FOUND, which tells the catalogue its publish never completed.

Expect 200 with active:true and the identity claims: user_id, org_id, entity_type, registries, given_name, family_name and email.

`registries` is a JSON array. If it ever comes back as a bare string, the realm's protocol mapper is not marked multivalued and Keycloak is silently sending only the FIRST value — re-run ./setup-realm.sh, which asserts against exactly that. When the user holds none, the key is null rather than [], because Keycloak omits an empty attribute altogether.

Entirely local: the signature is checked against Keycloak's published key, so there is no network call to Keycloak on the hot path. The token itself is never echoed back.

Denylists the token and its session, then ends the Keycloak session. refreshToken is optional.

Expect 200 with localRevocation:ok and idpLogout:ok.

The same access token as before. Expect 401 AUTH_TOKEN_REVOKED.

This is the point of the Redis denylist. A JWT is a self-contained signed string and Keycloak cannot recall one it has already issued, so without this the token would keep working until it expired and 'invalidate' would be a lie.

Blocks the account. The catalogue calls this on ACTIVE -> INACTIVE.

Expect 200 with revoked:true and keycloakDisabled:ok. Two things happen, and neither alone is enough: every live token is denylisted (Keycloak cannot recall an issued token), and the Keycloak user is disabled (otherwise the block would quietly wear off when the denylist entries expired).

Afterwards, Validate Token returns 401 for any token they held, and Create Token returns 403 AUTH_USER_DISABLED.

To undo it, call Create User again — that re-enables the user and clears the block. Tokens revoked here stay dead.

Removes the user from Keycloak and kills every token they hold. The catalogue calls this on delete.

Expect 200 with revoked:true and deleted:true. Revocation happens first, deliberately: deleting a Keycloak user does not invalidate a JWT it already signed, and once the user is gone there is nothing left to enumerate their sessions from.

Send it again and you get deleted:false with 200, not a 404 — a caller retrying a half-finished cleanup has to be able to complete it.

Expect 404 AUTH_USER_NOT_FOUND. Proves the user is really gone.

This is why a delete endpoint exists at all: since token creation needs only a userId, a user deleted from the catalogue but left behind in Keycloak could have tokens minted for them indefinitely.

The body Create Token takes once credential verification is switched on. NOT part of the top-to-bottom walkthrough — on a default stack it returns 400 AUTH_INVALID_REQUEST, because the flag alone selects the path and the default path wants {userId}.

To try it: set CATALOGUE_VALIDATE_ENABLED=true and CATALOGUE_BASE_URL to the user-catalogue, restart, and confirm the log says mode=VERIFIED. Then:

  valid:true  -> 200, and the token is for the userId the CATALOGUE returned
  valid:false -> 401 AUTH_INVALID_CREDENTIALS
  catalogue unreachable, or a body we cannot parse -> 503, never a token

The catalogue endpoint does not exist yet. Its contract is in README section 4.
